summary_grc: ὁ Ἀρίστων εἶπεν ὅτι μάχη οὐδεμία γένοιτο. χειμῶνος δὲ τοὺς ἀποθανόντας ἔθαψαν, καὶ ὁ Περικλῆς ἔλεγε τοιάδε.
summary_en: Autumn 431: Ariston marches with the whole army into the Megarid and comes home; in winter the city buries its first dead and Pericles speaks. The optative in indirect speech, the uses of the cases, and correlatives (τοιοῦτος … οἷος, τοσοῦτος … ὅσος); the opening of the Funeral Speech, Thucydides 2.35, adapted.
caption_grc: ὁ Λύσις ἤρετο εἰ μάχη γένοιτο. — ὁ στρατὸς τοσοῦτος ἦν ὅσος οὔποτε πρότερον.

original.note: Thucydides 2.35.1, the opening of Pericles' Funeral Speech, adapted in paragraph 3. Thucydides says he gives the speakers' words 'as each seemed to me to say what was needed', keeping as close as he could to what was actually said.

ἐν τούτοις ἦν καὶ ὁ Ἀρίστων ὁπλίτης, καὶ ὁ Σίμων ὁ μέτοικος. τὴν δὲ γῆν τῶν Μεγαρέων ἔτεμον ἀντὶ τῶν ἀγρῶν ὧν οἱ Λακεδαιμόνιοι ἔτεμον.

grammar.md:
**1. The optative in indirect speech.** After a **past** verb of saying or asking, the verb of a ὅτι-clause or an indirect question *may* change to the optative of the same tense (it may also stay as it was). The optative adds nothing to the meaning; it simply marks the words as reported:

| direct | reported after a past verb |
|---|---|
| «μάχη οὐδεμία ἐγένετο.» | εἶπεν ὅτι μάχη οὐδεμία **γένοιτο** (or ἐγένετο) |
| «ἆρα μάχη ἐγένετο;» | ἤρετο εἰ μάχη **γένοιτο** |
| «τί εἶπεν ὁ Περικλῆς;» | ἤρετο τί **εἴποι** ὁ Περικλῆς |
| «τὴν πόλιν ἐπαινεῖ.» | εἶπεν ὅτι τὴν πόλιν **ἐπαινοίη** |

Together with 9.3 this completes the rule of sequence: after a past main verb, subjunctives and indicatives in dependent clauses may become optatives.

**2. The cases, in full.** You have met each use separately; here they are side by side.

| case | use | example |
|---|---|---|
| genitive | possession, part of a whole | ἡ γῆ τῶν Μεγαρέων · μύριοι τῶν πολιτῶν · οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν εἰπόντων |
| | time within which | χειμῶνος 'in winter' · θέρους |
| | with prepositions of separation, ἀντί | ἐκ τῆς πόλεως · ἀντὶ τῶν ἀφανῶν |
| | with verbs (ἡγέομαι, ἀκούω, ἄρχω) | ἡγεῖτο αὐτῶν ὁ Περικλῆς |
| dative | indirect object, interest | οἱ οἰκεῖοι αὐτοῖς δῶρα ἔφερον |
| | means, instrument, manner | πάσῃ τῇ δυνάμει · ἔργῳ · δημοσίᾳ |
| | time when | τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ, τῷ χειμῶνι |
| accusative | direct object | τὴν γῆν ἔτεμον |
| | two objects (person and thing) | τοιαῦτα τοὺς Μεγαρέας ἐποιήσαμεν |
| | extent of time and space | δύο ἡμέρας · ἑξήκοντα σταδίους |
| | subject of an infinitive (9.1) | οἴομαι τοὺς Λακεδαιμονίους … καίειν |

**3. Correlatives.** Question words, demonstratives and relatives come in matching sets:

| question | 'this, so' | relative 'as, which' |
|---|---|---|
| ποῖος; of what sort? | **τοιοῦτος** (τοιόσδε) such | **οἷος** as, such as |
| πόσος; how big, how many? | **τοσοῦτος** so big, so many | **ὅσος** as big as, as many as |
| ποῦ; where? | ἐνταῦθα, ἐκεῖ there | οὗ where |
| πότε; when? | τότε then | ὅτε when |
| πῶς; how? | οὕτως so | ὡς as |

They are used in pairs: *ὁ στρατὸς τοσοῦτος ἦν ὅσος οὔποτε πρότερον* 'the army was as big as never before'; *οὐδεμία πόλις τοιαύτη ἐστὶν οἵα ἡ ἡμετέρα* 'no city is such as ours'. τοιοῦτος and τοσοῦτος decline like οὗτος (τοιοῦτος, τοιαύτη, τοιοῦτο(ν)); οἷος and ὅσος like καλός.

culture.title: The public funeral
culture.md:
Thucydides describes the Athenian custom (the πάτριος νόμος) for the war dead, as it was carried out in the winter of 431/0 for the first men killed in this war. The bones of the dead, cremated where they fell, were laid out in a tent for two days, and relatives brought offerings. Then wagons carried coffins of cypress wood, one for each of the ten tribes, with each man's bones in his own tribe's coffin, and one empty bier, spread with a cloth, for those whose bodies could not be recovered. Anyone who wished, citizen or foreigner, joined the procession; the women of the family lamented at the grave. The dead were buried in the public tomb (δημόσιον σῆμα) in the most beautiful suburb of the city, along the road from the Dipylon Gate through the outer Kerameikos, where Ariston's neighbours fired their pots. Only the dead of Marathon had been buried where they fell, for their outstanding courage. Their names were cut on marble lists, tribe by tribe, without father's name or deme: in death every citizen was equal.

Then a man chosen by the city for his judgement and standing spoke over them. In 431 it was **Pericles**. He stood on a high platform so that as many as possible could hear, and began, oddly, by doubting the custom of the speech itself: brave deeds, he says, should be honoured with deeds, and many men's courage should not depend on one speaker. Most of the speech that follows (2.35–46) praises not the dead but the city they died for, and it has been quoted ever since. Whether the words are Pericles' or Thucydides' is still argued.

With the funeral the first year of the war ends. From here on the course also opens **side readings** in four tracks, mythology, philosophy, history and politics, for you to follow alongside Units 10–12.
